conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. Today I’d like to do a quick, routine check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a short set of 10 questions that helps us see how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, so we can make sure you’re getting any support you might need.

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety. There are no right or wrong answers, and many new moms find some of the feelings pretty familiar. We’ll go through the questions one by one; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the things you used to look forward to, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Honestly? Not really. I used to love putting on music while I cooked, or going for a quick walk with a podcast, but lately it all feels like just one more chore. I’ll flip through the shows I used to binge and think, “What’s the point?” I still try—like, yesterday I sat down with my knitting—but after five minutes I felt so blah I just put it away. It’s like the color’s been drained out of everything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Mostly just “no, not much.” I mean, every now and then the baby will do something that makes me crack a tiny smile, but it fades fast. My husband will make a joke and I’ll force a little laugh so he doesn’t worry, but it doesn’t feel real. I can’t remember the last time I actually giggled or felt that light, happy feeling.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’d say “hardly ever.” I wake up thinking about all the feeds and diapers ahead and just feel… flat. Like, my sister keeps texting about brunch next week, and normally I’d be excited, but right now it just sounds exhausting. I still try to plan little things, but the spark isn’t there—it’s more like I’m ticking boxes so people won’t worry.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah, that happens to me a lot—definitely “yes, some of the time.” When the baby wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. yesterday, I kept thinking, “I’m doing something wrong; a good mom would know how to calm him.” If I spill a little pumped milk or forget to pack a burp cloth, I replay it all day and feel like I’ve failed him. Even when my husband says the baby’s gaining fine, I still worry my mistakes are holding him back.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often—I'd say “yes, very often.” My mind keeps racing with all the what-ifs: what if he stops breathing in his sleep, what if I miss some sign that he's sick, what if I'm not making enough milk even though the pediatrician says he's gaining fine. Sometimes I'll just be sitting there and this wave of dread hits me out of nowhere, and I have to check him three times to calm down a little.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes—maybe “yes, sometimes.” Every so often my heart just starts racing and I feel like something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. Last night I was rocking the baby in the dark and suddenly I was sure I couldn’t breathe right and had to put him in the crib so I could sit down and concentrate on taking slow breaths. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah... “Yes, sometimes I haven’t been coping as well as usual.” There are stretches—like yesterday when he wouldn’t nap and the laundry was piled up—where I feel like I’m drowning. I’ll just stand in the kitchen staring at the mess, not sure what to tackle first, and end up crying while I fold onesies. I still get the essentials done, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

“Yes, most of the time.” I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with worries about the baby, tomorrow’s chores, all the ways I’m probably messing up. Even when he sleeps a four-hour stretch, I wake up every hour checking the monitor, heart pounding. By the time I do drift off, it’s almost time for the next feed, so I’m running on crumbs.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… “yes, most of the time” fits. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a gray cloud parked over me. Little things—seeing a cute outfit he’ll outgrow, hearing a lullaby—make me tear up. I wouldn’t call it crying spells every single moment, but the sadness is just… there, humming in the background while I do bottles, diapers, everything.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

“Yes, sometimes.” I don’t cry every single day, but maybe three or four times this week. Yesterday was the worst—he wouldn’t latch, I spilled the pumped milk I’d spent 20 minutes getting, and I just sat on the nursery floor with him on my lap and bawled. It feels like the tears are right under the surface, and any little frustration tips them over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… that hasn’t crossed my mind. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared how the joy you once found in music, walks, or knitting has faded, replaced by a flat heaviness that makes even planning brunch feel exhausting. Over the past week you've forced smiles, cried over spilled milk, and felt your heart race with nameless dread while checking the monitor all night. Despite these struggles, you continue to care devotedly for your baby and bravely reached out for help-an important step for any new mom.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports virtually no genuine laughter, only forced smiles/laughs and absence of light, happy feeling, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "hardly ever" and describes pervasive loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly aligns with "yes, some of the time" and gives multiple examples of self-blame over minor issues.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "yes, very often" and describes racing thoughts, persistent what-ifs, and sudden waves of dread, aligning with the highest anxiety frequency option.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly says "yes, sometimes" and describes classic panic episodes (racing heart, breathlessness) that occur "every so often" but not continuously, aligning with "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly quotes the option "Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual" and provides vivid examples of feeling overwhelmed yet still managing essentials.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly chose "Yes, most of the time" and detailed nightly insomnia with racing worries, frequent waking to check monitor, and minimal restorative sleep despite exhaustion.</sym>, <sym>Patient directly endorses "yes, most of the time," describes pervasive low mood and tearfulness throughout daily activities.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 22 exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</sm>: most-day low mood and anhedonia (<quote>the color's been drained</quote>), plus five additional symptoms including guilt (<quote>I've failed him</quote>), psychomotor agitation (<quote>heart racing</quote>), fatigue, concentration difficulty, and insomnia unrelated to infant care. Frequent crying, feeling overwhelmed, and excessive worry also suggest comorbid postpartum anxiety. Absence of self-harm thoughts lowers immediate safety risk but does not reduce clinical urgency. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>OB-GYN</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> this week
2. Bring this EPDS result to your visit; ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or safe antidepressant options while breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 15-minute mood-boosting activity, even if motivation is low-pleasant music, brief outdoor stroll, or virtual coffee with a friend
4. Follow simple sleep-hygiene: trade night shifts with partner when possible, keep lights dim during feeds, and postpone chores to maximize rest
5. Schedule pediatric or lactation follow-up to address latch/milk-supply worries feeding anxiety
6. Reach out to local support groups or hotlines like Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4PPD) for parent-peer encouragement
7. If distress escalates or you ever think of self-harm, call 988 or your local emergency number immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: **Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Summary**

**Symptoms endorsed**  
- Persistent low mood, sadness “most of the time”  
- Marked loss of pleasure/enjoyment (“hardly ever” looks forward to activities)  
- Frequent crying spells (3–4× this week)  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt regarding parenting adequacy  
- Recurrent intrusive worries, nocturnal checking, physiologic panic symptoms (palpitations, breathlessness)  
- Sleep disturbance driven by anxious rumination rather than infant schedule  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “drowning” in daily tasks  

**Pattern**  
Symptoms cluster into depressive (affect, pleasure, tearfulness) and anxiety (worry, panic, hypervigilance) domains, present “most/sometimes” over the past week, causing functional difficulty but without self-harm ideation.

**Screening significance**  
Score pattern and clinical descriptors are consistent with probable major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; further evaluation (diagnostic interview, PHQ-9/EPDS, suicide risk probe) warranted.

**Safety**  
Patient denies suicidal or self-harm thoughts at present; no acute safety concern identified from this screen.
